sentences.text: The brief facts of the case are that the revisionist / complainant had filed a complaint against respondent no.2 Sanjay Kumar wherein allegations of committing of offences of criminal trespass, cheating and forgery of documents have been leveled against respondent no.2 Sanjay Kumar.

As per the complaint of revisionist /complainant, respondent no.2 Sanjay Kumar had approached the complainant to sell his commercial property with roof rights situated at 111, Pocket-J, Sector- 14, Bawana Industrial Complex, Rohini, Delhi-110039 measuring 250 square meters.

That the complainant, after visiting the property and inspection of the chain of title documents, agreed to purchase the afore-mentioned property for a total consideration of Rs.49,50,000/- from respondent no.2.
That symbolic possession of the property was given by respondent no.2 to revisionist/complaint by handing over the keys of property.
That the parties executed registered GPA, SPA, Deed of Sale Agreement, Receipt and other documents.

Thereafter, respondent no.2 requested the complainant to hand over the keys of the property in question for three days for shifting his machinery and other articles lying in the afore-mentioned property which was duly handed over by complainant to respondent no.2.
That in the meantime, complainant got electricity connection in his name and the property in question.

Thereafter, on 25.12.2021, when complainant Digitally signed by SUSHIL Rakesh Sehgal Vs. State & Anr. SUSHIL KUMAR KUMAR Date:

Respondent no.2 Sanjay Kumar filed reply / written submissions to the present revision petition wherein he claimed that the execution of documents pertaining to property in question were just a formality to secure financial help and that the petitioner induced the respondent no.2 to sign / execute documents with an intention to commit fraud and cheating upon respondent no.2.

It is argued on behalf of respondent no.2 that property documents were executed as a collateral security for friendly loan of Rs.50,00,000/- given by revisionist/complainant and it was agreed that the documents shall be returned after return of loan amount.

5. This Court has given thoughtful consideration to the arguments advanced on behalf of Ld.
Counsel for the revisionist/complainant as well as Ld. Counsel for the respondents/accused persons and also perused the material available on record.

6. It is trite in law that when criminal complaint is filed before the Magistrate and upon perusal it is found that it discloses a cognizable offence having been committed, two courses are open to the Magistrate.

He may chose to inquire into the complaint by taking cognizance in exercise of his powers under Section 190 Cr.P.C. and proceed to inquire into it in accordance with the procedure laid down in Sections 200 and 202 Cr.P.C.
In the alternative, he may refer the complaint to police under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. for investigation.
In the latter case, the Magistrate having given such direction would stay his hand till report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. is submitted by the police, on which further process of law would follow.
Digitally  signed by  SUSHIL  SUSHIL KUMAR  KUMAR

Date:
Rakesh Sehgal Vs. State & Anr. 2024.08.14  16:23:14 7.
The Magistrate is not supposed to act mechanically and direct registration of FIR in each and every case in routine and casual manner.
Criminal law is not expected to be set in motion on mere asking of a party.

There has to be some substance in the complaint filed and it is only if it appears that the allegations are serious enough and establish the commission of cognizable offence required thorough investigation by the police, an FIR should be ordered to be registered.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as "Lalita Kumari Vs. State of U.P"., (2014) 2 SCC 1, have laid down certain guidelines and certain directions have been issued to the police with regard to the registration of FIRs.

"120.6.
As to what type and in which cases preliminary inquiry is to be conducted will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The category of cases in which preliminary inquiry may be made are as under : -
(a) Matrimonial disputes/family disputes (b) Commercial offences (c) Medical negligence cases (d) Corruption cases (e) Cases where there is abnormal delay/ laches in initiating criminal prosecution, for example, over 3 months' delay in reporting the matter without satisfactorily explaining the reasons for delay."

It has been argued on behalf of revisionist/complainant that registration of FIR is necessary for conducting thorough investigation with respect to execution of documents such as GPA, SPA, Deed of Sale Agreement etc., as well as for recovery of the cheated amount, therefore, directions for registration of FIR may kindly be issued and the impugned order passed by Ld. MM concerned may kindly be set- aside.

9. After perusal of the record including the Trial Record Record and after considering submissions of Ld. Counsels for both parties, this Court is of considered view that in the present case, prima facie, it appears that the complainant has been cheated for Rs.49,50,000/- by respondent no.2 Sanjay Kumar and FIR ought to have been registered since scientific investigation / recovery is needed to be done by the police, therefore, the impugned order dated 21.12.2022 is hereby set-aside and SHO PS Bawana is directed to register an FIR and to investigate the matter in proper manner.
